ICU progress note, hospital day 2. The patient is a 40-year-old female admitted with acute kidney injury from dehydration after four days of vomiting and poor oral intake from presumed viral gastroenteritis. She has no chronic medical conditions and takes no medications at home. She was hypotensive on arrival and was admitted to the ICU for close monitoring.

Overnight events: none. She slept well and her vomiting has stopped. She tolerated sips of clear liquids and says she feels less thirsty and less lightheaded than yesterday. She denies abdominal pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, and confusion.

Current treatment: lactated Ringer's infusion at 125 mL per hour and ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 hours as needed for nausea, of which she needed one dose overnight. Urine output over the last 24 hours was 1.1 L.

Vitals this morning: temperature 37.0 C, heart rate 88, blood pressure 112/68, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Weight is 64 kg.

Exam: mucous membranes are moist, there is no jugular venous distension, the lungs are clear, the abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no leg edema.

Lab trend: creatinine 2.4 mg/dL on admission, 1.9 mg/dL yesterday, and 1.5 mg/dL this morning, with a baseline of 0.8 mg/dL. BUN has fallen from 42 to 24. Potassium is 3.6 and sodium is 138. Urinalysis was bland. Renal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis.

Impression: acute kidney injury due to dehydration, prerenal in type, improving with fluids. Going forward, I will reduce lactated Ringer's to 75 mL per hour, repeat a basic metabolic panel this afternoon and tomorrow morning, avoid NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins, advance her diet as tolerated, and stop ondansetron if she has no further nausea. If creatinine continues to fall, she can transfer out of the ICU to the floor tomorrow.

Creatinine has improved from 2.4 to 1.5 mg/dL against a baseline of 0.8, and renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis. She is receiving lactated Ringer's and ondansetron as needed. The plan is to reduce the fluid rate, repeat a basic metabolic panel, avoid nephrotoxins, advance her diet, and consider transfer to the floor tomorrow.

note:
Cardiology clinic follow-up for a 55-year-old female seen three weeks after an acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with a drug-eluting stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery. Her history includes paroxysmal atrial fibrillation diagnosed two years ago, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, and she has taken an anticoagulant for the atrial fibrillation since the diagnosis. She has no known drug allergies.

Since discharge she has felt well. She walks 20 minutes daily without chest pain, and she denies shortness of breath, palpitations, lightheadedness, and syncope. She has noticed easy bruising on both forearms, but she denies black stools, blood in the urine, nosebleeds, and gum bleeding.

On medication review she first told me she takes apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily. When she read the label on her bottle, she corrected this to apixaban 5 mg twice daily, which is the dose her primary care physician prescribed and is appropriate for her age, weight, and kidney function. The other medications she brought in are clopidogrel 75 mg daily and aspirin 81 mg daily, both started at discharge, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly and metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily, also started at discharge, and her long-standing lisinopril 10 mg daily and metformin 1000 mg twice daily.

Because lisinopril and atorvastatin are not safe in pregnancy, I reviewed her reproductive status. She is postmenopausal, with her last menstrual period about 14 months ago, and the urine pregnancy test done in the hospital was negative. Pregnancy is therefore not a concern for her current or planned prescribing, and she does not need contraception.

Blood pressure today was 126/74 with a heart rate of 64 and oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Weight is 82 kg. Jugular venous pressure is normal, rhythm is regular without murmur, lungs are clear, and there is no leg edema. The right radial access site is well healed, and she has a few small ecchymoses on both forearms. ECG today shows sinus rhythm at 62 with anterior T-wave inversions and no new changes. The inpatient echocardiogram showed an LVEF of 45% with anterior hypokinesis. Labs from this week show LDL cholesterol 96 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, potassium 4.3, and hemoglobin A1c 7.4%.

My impression is that she is recovering well from an anterior STEMI with stent placement, with mildly reduced LVEF and an LDL still above goal. Her bleeding risk is elevated on triple antithrombotic therapy, which accounts for the bruising. Her blood pressure and diabetes are acceptable.

I stopped the aspirin today and will continue clopidogrel 75 mg daily together with apixaban 5 mg twice daily; clopidogrel will continue for 12 months from the stent, after which apixaban alone will be used. I increased atorvastatin from 40 mg to 80 mg nightly and increased metoprolol succinate from 25 mg to 50 mg daily. I started pantoprazole 40 mg daily for stomach protection while she is on two antithrombotic drugs. Lisinopril and metformin are unchanged. She is referred to cardiac rehabilitation. I ordered a repeat lipid panel in six weeks, and if LDL remains above 55 mg/dL I will add ezetimibe. A repeat echocardiogram is planned in three months to reassess LVEF. She will call or go to the emergency department for chest pain, fainting, or any significant bleeding. Follow-up in clinic in four weeks.

She has no chest pain or bleeding symptoms apart from easy bruising, and her apixaban dose was clarified as 5 mg twice daily. Aspirin was stopped, atorvastatin and metoprolol succinate were increased, and pantoprazole was started. Cardiac rehabilitation, a repeat lipid panel, and a repeat echocardiogram were arranged, with follow-up in four weeks.

HPI:

- takes Tums for heartburn, ~6-8/day x 2 mo

- no hx cancer, no wt loss, no night sweats
- NKDA

Meds PTA:
- HCTZ 25 mg daily
- lisinopril 20 mg daily
- calcium carbonate 500 mg, 6-8 tabs/day (Tums)
- vit D3 2000 units daily

Vitals: T 98.2 F, HR 82, BP 148/90, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, wt 88 kg

Exam:
- NAD, mildly dry MM
- neck: no palpable thyroid nodule or mass
- RRR, no murmur
- lungs CTA
- abd soft, NT, ND, no CVA tenderness
- neuro: A&O x 3, no focal deficit, DTRs normal

- Ca 13.4 (ref 8.6-10.3), albumin 4.2
- iPTH 142 pg/mL -- elevated, not suppressed

- 25-OH vit D 28
- ECG: NSR 80, short QT, no arrhythmia
- renal US: nonobstructing 4 mm R renal stone, no hydronephrosis

A/P:
1. Primary hyperparathyroidism w/ symptomatic hypercalcemia (Ca 13.4), PTH-mediated
2. Mild AKI, prerenal from volume depletion + hypercalcemia, Cr 1.3
3. HTN -- thiazide, Tums, and vit D all likely contributing to Ca
- NS 1 L bolus then 150 mL/h

ED labs showed an elevated iPTH of 142 pg/mL, low phosphorus, and creatinine 1.3, and renal ultrasound showed a nonobstructing right renal stone. The impression was primary hyperparathyroidism with symptomatic hypercalcemia and mild acute kidney injury. He was started on normal saline, HCTZ, calcium carbonate, and vit D3 were stopped, amlodipine was started, and he was placed in observation with outpatient parathyroid workup and surgical referral.

note:
Telehealth visit note, orthopedics. Visit type: audio-only telephone visit. The patient is an 82-year-old male calling from home. His identity was confirmed with two identifiers and he consented to a telephone visit. His daughter was on the line, with his permission, to help with the medication list. He is being seen for follow-up of a left distal radius fracture.

History: He fell on an icy step six weeks ago and landed on his outstretched left hand. He first said the fall was four weeks ago, but his daughter reminded him that the cast was applied the day of the fall, and the clinic record confirms this, so the correct interval is six weeks. The injury was a closed, minimally displaced left distal radius fracture, treated in a short-arm cast. The cast was removed at his visit last week and he was placed in a removable wrist splint.

Today he reports wrist pain of 2 out of 10 at rest and 4 out of 10 when gripping, improved from 7 out of 10 at the time of injury. He wears the splint most of the day and removes it to wash. He has some stiffness in the fingers in the morning that eases within a few minutes. He denies numbness, tingling, finger swelling, fever, new falls, easy bruising, and black stools. He can make a full fist and touch his thumb to each fingertip, which he demonstrated to his daughter.

Medications, read from the bottles by his daughter: apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, and tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. At the time of injury he was prescribed tramadol and acetaminophen. He first said he took tramadol 100 mg, then corrected himself after reading the bottle to tramadol 50 mg every 6 hours as needed. He stopped the tramadol a week ago because it made him dizzy and constipated, so it is discontinued. He takes acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed. He admitted that since the cast came off he has also taken ibuprofen 400 mg once or twice a day for the wrist. He has no known drug allergies.

Home measurements: BP 134/78 and HR 68 on his home cuff. Weight was not checked today.

Limited exam: no visual exam was possible by telephone. Per the patient and his daughter, there is mild swelling at the wrist, no visible deformity, no redness, and no skin breakdown under the splint, and he can wiggle all five fingers.

Data: Wrist radiographs at last week's visit showed a healing left distal radius fracture with early callus and maintained alignment, with volar tilt of 8 degrees and preserved radial height. Labs from his primary care visit last month showed creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, eGFR 62, and vitamin D 22 ng/mL, which is low. He has never had a bone density scan.

Impression: Left distal radius fracture, healing well at six weeks after a fall. This is a fragility fracture, so I am concerned about underlying osteoporosis, and his vitamin D insufficiency needs treatment. He has atrial fibrillation on apixaban, so avoiding NSAIDs is important to prevent bleeding.

Recommendations: He should stop the ibuprofen today, and I explained that it raises his bleeding risk with apixaban. I increased acetaminophen to 1000 mg three times daily as needed, up from 500 mg every 6 hours as needed, not to exceed 3000 mg a day. I started vitamin D3 1000 units daily and ordered a DEXA scan. He will continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily without interruption. He will wean off the splint over the next two weeks, start outpatient occupational therapy for range of motion and grip strength, and avoid lifting more than 5 pounds for four more weeks. I will repeat radiographs of the left wrist at an in-person clinic visit in four weeks. He and his daughter understand and will call for numbness, severe pain, any bleeding, or a new fall.

Ibuprofen was stopped, acetaminophen was increased, vitamin D3 was started, and a DEXA scan, hand therapy, and repeat radiographs in four weeks were arranged.

note:
The patient is a 71-year-old male seen in the cardiology clinic for follow-up of statin intolerance with persistently high LDL cholesterol. He has established coronary artery disease with a bypass operation eight years ago, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and heavy alcohol use. He lives alone and has little social support; his only relative is a son who lives in another state and calls on weekends. He has no known drug allergies.

Over the past two years he developed muscle aching in both thighs and shoulders on atorvastatin 40 mg, and again on rosuvastatin 10 mg, and each time the aching improved within about three weeks of stopping. For the past three months he has taken rosuvastatin 5 mg three times a week, but he still has aching in both thighs and says he skips doses when the pain is bad. He denies muscle weakness, dark urine, and chest pain, and he denies shortness of breath, palpitations, and lightheadedness.

He drinks about five beers every evening and sometimes more on weekends, and his last drink was the night before this visit. He denies tremor, hallucinations, and seizures when he goes without drinking. He does not smoke. He has no one to drive him and came by bus, and he says some days he does not eat a full meal because shopping is hard for him.

For medication reconciliation he first told me he takes aspirin 325 mg daily, but when he emptied his pill bag onto the exam table the bottle read aspirin 81 mg, so the correct dose is 81 mg daily. His other medications are metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and metformin 500 mg twice daily, along with the rosuvastatin 5 mg three times a week.

Blood pressure was 148/86 with a heart rate of 66, and weight was 84 kg. Heart sounds are regular without murmur, lungs are clear, and there is no edema. There is no tenderness over the thighs or shoulders and strength is 5 out of 5 in all major muscle groups. He has no tremor or diaphoresis, and the sternotomy scar is well healed. Labs drawn last week on rosuvastatin 5 mg show total cholesterol 218 mg/dL, LDL cholesterol 142 mg/dL, HDL 41 mg/dL, triglycerides 186 mg/dL, AST 52 U/L, ALT 41 U/L, CK 118 U/L, hemoglobin A1c 7.1%, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, and eGFR 68.

My impression is statin intolerance with muscle symptoms on two different statins, with an LDL far above the goal of 55 mg/dL for his coronary disease. He also has heavy alcohol use with a mildly elevated AST, blood pressure above goal, and social isolation.

I stopped rosuvastatin today because it is not controlling his LDL and causes aching. I started ezetimibe 10 mg daily and bempedoic acid 180 mg daily. Because his LDL will likely stay above goal on these, I will begin the prior authorization for evolocumab as the next step. I increased amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily for his blood pressure and started thiamine 100 mg daily. We discussed cutting down on alcohol, and he agreed to meet with a counselor. I referred him to social work for home meal delivery and transportation vouchers so that he can attend visits. I ordered a repeat lipid panel and liver tests in eight weeks, and he will return in 12 weeks.
summary: A 71-year-old male with coronary artery disease with prior bypass surgery, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and heavy alcohol use, who lives alone with little support, was seen for statin intolerance and high LDL. He developed muscle aching on atorvastatin and rosuvastatin and still has thigh aching on low-dose rosuvastatin, with LDL cholesterol 142 mg/dL and a mildly elevated AST. His aspirin dose was clarified as 81 mg daily. Rosuvastatin was stopped, ezetimibe and bempedoic acid were started, amlodipine was increased, and thiamine was started. He was referred to social work for meals and transportation, with repeat lipid and liver tests in eight weeks.

Doctor: Good morning. I see you're a 70-year-old female here to talk about your cholesterol results and whether you should start a statin. How are you feeling today?
Patient: A little nervous, honestly. I've been reading online about those cholesterol pills, and I read they can destroy your muscles and your memory and your liver. Is that true? My neighbor had to stop hers.
Doctor: Those are very reasonable questions, and I'll go through each one. First, do you have any muscle pain, weakness, chest pain, or shortness of breath right now?
Patient: No muscle pain, no chest pain, and I'm not short of breath. My knees ache from arthritis, but that's all. Oh, and I forget where I put my glasses sometimes. Is that the memory thing already?
Doctor: No, that's very common and not caused by anything you're taking. Any yellow skin, dark urine, or belly pain?
Patient: No, nothing like that. Can I ask one more thing? What if I start it and feel worse?
Doctor: Then you stop it and call us. Let's go through your medicines. What are you taking?
Patient: Metformin 500 mg twice a day. No, wait, 1000 mg twice a day, the doctor raised it last year. Lisinopril 10 mg every morning, omeprazole 20 mg every day for reflux, and ibuprofen 400 mg most days for my knees.
Doctor: Anything else, like acetaminophen or supplements? Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: Acetaminophen 500 mg once in a while. No allergies.
Doctor: And how much alcohol do you drink in a typical week?
Patient: Oh, a glass of wine with dinner. Well, if I'm honest, three or four glasses of wine every evening. Is that bad for the cholesterol?
Doctor: That counts as heavy drinking for a woman, and it matters for your liver, blood pressure, and triglycerides. We'll come back to that. Any family history of heart disease?
Patient: My father had a heart attack at 62. I worry about that all the time.
Doctor: I understand. Your blood pressure today is 148/86, pulse 78, and weight 74 kilograms. Your heart and lungs sound normal, and there is no swelling in your legs. Your knees are mildly stiff and tender but not swollen. Your labs from last week show total cholesterol 262, LDL 168, HDL 48, triglycerides 230, AST 36 and ALT 30, which are both normal, so your liver is fine for now. Your A1c is 7.3 and creatinine is 0.9.

I'll order a repeat lipid panel and liver tests in 8 weeks, a kidney panel and potassium two weeks after the lisinopril change, and a nurse will call you in 2 weeks to ask about muscle aches. Doctor: Hi, come on in. I have you down as a 14-year-old male here for acne, and I see your grandmother came with you.
Family member: Yes, I'm his grandmother. I take care of him during the week because his mom works nights, so I'll tell you what I know and he can fill in the rest.
Doctor: Great. How long has the acne been going on?
Patient: About a year, mostly on my forehead, cheeks, and back. It got a lot worse in the last three months.
Family member: It's painful for him, too. Some of the bumps on his cheeks are big and red.
Doctor: Do those bumps hurt?
Patient: The big ones do, yeah. I have a few marks left on my cheeks too.

Patient: A salicylic acid face wash from the store, but it made my face dry and red, so I stopped it two weeks ago. I use a benzoyl peroxide wash every day. And the adapalene gel from my pediatrician.
Family member: He puts the adapalene on every night, I make sure.
Patient: Grandma, no, I only use it about twice a week because it burns.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. So the adapalene is really twice a week. Is it the 0.1% gel?
Patient: Yeah.
Doctor: Any other medical problems or medicines?
Family member: He has asthma. He uses an albuterol inhaler when he needs it, and a fluticasone inhaler, two puffs twice a day. And his ADHD medicine, methylphenidate ER, 54 mg every morning.
Patient: Gran, it's 36 mg. The bottle says 36.
Family member: Oh, you're right, 36 mg. I mixed it up with his old dose.

Patient: No fever, no joint pain, and I'm not sad or anything. I drink a protein shake after football practice, most days.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?

There are also papules across the upper back. There is mild dark discoloration where old spots healed, but no deep scarring. His blood pressure is 112/68 and his weight is 58 kilograms. The pediatrician's labs from three weeks ago show ALT 22, creatinine 0.7, and hemoglobin 14.2, all normal.

Start doxycycline 100 mg twice a day with food and a full glass of water for 12 weeks, and use sunscreen because it makes you sunburn easily. Keep the benzoyl peroxide wash daily. For the adapalene, use a pea-size amount every other night with a moisturizer for two weeks, then every night, instead of twice a week. Stop the salicylic acid wash. She was seen at an urgent care two days ago, where albuterol 2 puffs by spacer every 4 hours as needed was prescribed, but her mother saw no benefit.

On examination, temperature was 38.0 C, heart rate 152, respiratory rate 52, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Weight was 8.2 kg, down from 8.6 kg at her six-month visit. Mucous membranes are slightly dry, capillary refill is 2 seconds, and the anterior fontanelle is flat. Tympanic membranes are clear and there is no rash. A rapid RSV antigen test was positive.

I recommended acetaminophen 120 mg every 6 hours as needed for fever or discomfort, which is about 15 mg/kg. No cough and cold medicines or honey. She will be rechecked in clinic tomorrow for weight and work of breathing. Her mother will take her to the emergency department for faster or harder breathing, pauses in breathing, bluish color, or no wet diaper in 8 hours.

Fatigue, non-restorative sleep, brain fog, and AM stiffness of about 20 minutes. Denies fever, wt loss, jaw claudication, new headache, vision change, scalp tenderness, joint swelling, rash, dry eyes, dry mouth, Raynaud's, proximal weakness, trouble rising from chair, dark urine, CP, SOB, trauma, and falls. PMH fibromyalgia, HTN, hypothyroidism, OA. Meds: duloxetine 30 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, OTC naproxen 440 mg BID for 2 weeks, acetaminophen 500 mg PRN. NKDA.
soap.objective: T 98.4 F, HR 74, BP 138/82, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA. Uncomfortable but in no acute distress, A&O. Diffuse tenderness at the neck, trapezius, lateral epicondyles, greater trochanters, and knees with no focal swelling; no synovitis, full ROM; strength 5/5 proximally and distally; temporal arteries nontender with palpable pulses; no rash; regular rhythm, lungs clear. ESR 14, CRP 0.4 mg/dL, CK 88, TSH 2.2; WBC 6.5, Hgb 12.8, plt 240; Na 140, K 4.0, Cr 0.9, Ca 9.5, glucose 98; UA negative.
soap.assessment: Fibromyalgia flare, clinical diagnosis, with no red flags for PMR or GCA, no inflammatory arthritis, and no myositis. HTN with BP 138/82, acceptable.
plan: Increase duloxetine from 30 mg to 60 mg daily.
Stop naproxen because of HTN, age, and renal risk.
Acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN, max 3 g/day.
Gentle walking 10 min/day, increased slowly, plus sleep hygiene.
Continue levothyroxine 75 mcg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily.
Discharge home from the ED.
Follow up in rheum clinic in 2-3 wk.
Return to the ED for fever, vision changes, jaw pain, severe headache, or weakness.

Doctor: Hello, I see you're a 45-year-old female here for a follow-up of your Parkinson's disease. What brought you to urgent care today?
Patient: My neurologist can't see me for two months, and my pills have been wearing off before the next dose. My right hand shakes more in the late afternoon and I feel stiff.
Doctor: How are you taking your medicine?
Patient: Carbidopa-levodopa 25/100, one tablet three times a day. And rasagiline 1 mg once a day.
Doctor: Any falls, dizziness when you stand up, hallucinations, or trouble swallowing?
Patient: No falls, no dizziness, no hallucinations, and swallowing is fine.
Doctor: Good. Your blood pressure is 118/74 sitting and 114/72 standing, with a pulse of 72. On exam you have a mild resting tremor in the right hand, mild stiffness in the right arm, slowed finger tapping on the right, and reduced arm swing on the right when you walk. Your balance on the pull test is normal.
Patient: So are the pills not working?
Doctor: They are working, but the effect is wearing off early. My impression is Parkinson's disease with mild end-of-dose wearing off. I will increase carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 to one tablet four times a day, spaced about four hours apart, and continue rasagiline 1 mg once a day. I would also like you to join a physical therapy program focused on movement and walking, and I will send a note to your neurologist asking to see you sooner. Come back or call if you have falls, hallucinations, or severe nausea.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 45-year-old female with Parkinson's disease presented to urgent care because her neurologist could not see her for two months and her medication was wearing off before the next dose, with more right hand shaking and stiffness in the late afternoon. She denied falls, dizziness, hallucinations, and trouble swallowing. Exam showed a mild right resting tremor, right arm stiffness, slowed finger tapping, reduced arm swing, and a normal pull test. The impression was Parkinson's disease with mild end-of-dose wearing off. Carbidopa-levodopa was increased to four times daily, rasagiline was continued, and physical therapy and an earlier neurology visit were arranged.

Telehealth visit note, geriatrics. Visit modality: audio-only telephone visit. The patient is a 90-year-old female speaking from her home. Her daughter, who is her designated health care surrogate, joined the call with the patient's permission. Identity was verified and the patient has decision-making capacity. The visit was for advance care planning and review of her chronic conditions, with a check after recent travel.

Interval history: She returned 10 days ago from a two-week overseas trip to visit her sister, including an 11-hour flight each way. She reports mild ankle swelling since the flight that is slowly improving. She denies calf pain, chest pain, shortness of breath beyond her baseline, fever, diarrhea, and cough. Her appetite is fair and she walks around the house with her walker. Her chronic conditions are heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, and osteoarthritis.

Medications confirmed with her daughter reading the bottles: furosemide 20 mg daily, apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily, and diphenhydramine 25 mg at bedtime, which she uses for sleep.

Home measurements: BP 124/70, HR 72, weight 54.3 kg on her home scale, up 1.2 kg from her usual 53.1 kg. No visual exam was possible by phone. Her daughter reports 1+ pitting swelling of both ankles with no difference between the legs. Labs drawn last week showed creatinine 1.5 mg/dL and potassium 4.4.

Advance care planning: We spent about 25 minutes discussing her goals. She wants to stay in her own home, avoid long hospital stays and machines, and would accept hospital treatment for reversible problems such as infection. She does not want CPR or a breathing tube if her heart stops. She confirmed that her daughter is her health care surrogate, and her advance directive on file reflects this. Both the patient and her daughter verbalized understanding.

Impression: Advance care planning completed, with a preference for DNR/DNI and selective treatment. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction with mild fluid retention after travel. Chronic kidney disease stage 3b, stable.

Recommendations: Increase furosemide from 20 mg to 40 mg daily for 3 days, then return to 20 mg daily. Stop diphenhydramine because of confusion and fall risk and start melatonin 3 mg at bedtime. Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily and metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily. Repeat a basic metabolic panel in one week. Weigh daily and call for a gain of more than 1 kg in 2 days. Elevate the legs when sitting. I will complete a POLST form and mail it for signature, and I will call her in two weeks, with an in-person visit in three months.

Furosemide was temporarily increased, diphenhydramine was stopped and melatonin started, and a basic metabolic panel, POLST form, and follow-up were arranged.

This is a dictation for a rheumatology inpatient follow-up on the hospital ward for a 77-year-old male with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, now hospital day 3, admitted with right lower lobe community-acquired pneumonia. He also has COPD, hypertension, and stage 3a chronic kidney disease, and he currently smokes one pack of cigarettes a day. He has no known drug allergies.

No overnight events. His cough is improving and he is no longer short of breath at rest. He reports morning stiffness in both hands lasting about 90 minutes and swelling of both wrists, worse since admission. He denies fever now, chest pain, hemoptysis, rash, mouth sores, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

For medication reconciliation, the admission list says methotrexate 15 mg once weekly, correction, 20 mg once weekly according to the bottle his neighbor brought in, taken with folic acid 1 mg daily. His other home medications are prednisone 5 mg daily, hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, a tiotropium inhaler once daily, and naproxen 500 mg twice daily from his primary care physician. In the hospital he is receiving ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, day three of five, and I ordered a nicotine patch 21 mg every 24 hours.

Vitals this morning temperature 99.1 F, heart rate 88, blood pressure 138/80, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 94% on room air. On exam both wrists are swollen and warm with tenderness, and he has six swollen and eight tender joints in the hands and wrists, with a rheumatoid nodule over the left olecranon. Crackles are present at the right base. There is no rash and no oral ulcers.

Labs today show white blood cell count 11.8 down from 14.2, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, platelets 342, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL up from his baseline of 1.3, ALT 31, AST 28, ESR 62, and CRP 7.8 mg/dL. Procalcitonin was 0.9. Chest x-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation, and the CT chest shows no interstitial lung disease and no ground-glass opacities, so methotrexate lung toxicity is unlikely.

My impression is first, a rheumatoid arthritis flare of moderate activity in the setting of pneumonia. Second, community-acquired pneumonia, improving on antibiotics. Third, creatinine above baseline, which matters because methotrexate is cleared by the kidneys and he has been taking naproxen. Fourth, current tobacco use.

Plan is as follows. I am holding methotrexate until the pneumonia has resolved and creatinine is back to baseline, then restarting at a lower dose of 15 mg once weekly. Continue folic acid 1 mg daily and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily. I am increasing prednisone from 5 mg to 10 mg daily for the flare and will taper back to 5 mg after discharge. I am stopping naproxen permanently because of his kidney function, the methotrexate interaction, and the steroid. Continue the nicotine patch 21 mg every 24 hours, and he was counseled on quitting.

Because transportation is a barrier, he lives about 60 miles from the clinic, has no car, and depends on a neighbor for rides, I asked social work to arrange transportation vouchers. His rheumatology follow-up in two weeks will be by video visit, and he will have a CBC, creatinine, and liver tests drawn one week after discharge at a lab near his home. I will see him in the clinic in six weeks if he can arrange a ride.
summary: A 77-year-old male with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, COPD, hypertension, stage 3a chronic kidney disease, and current tobacco use was seen on hospital day 3 of admission for right lower lobe pneumonia, with a rheumatoid arthritis flare of morning stiffness and wrist swelling. His methotrexate dose was corrected to 20 mg weekly. Exam showed six swollen and eight tender joints, ESR 62, CRP 7.8 mg/dL, and creatinine above baseline, and CT showed no interstitial lung disease. Methotrexate was held, prednisone was increased to 10 mg daily, naproxen was stopped, and a nicotine patch was started. Social work will arrange transportation, with a video rheumatology visit in two weeks and local labs.
